query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing an ultrathin, continuous graphene coating on the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 MM′X alloy will arrest crack propagation and enhance its mechanical integrity (e.g., compressive strength) while preserving its large applied-field and pressure-induced caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibiting excellent caloric performance but poor structural integrity and a tendency to crack under mechanical loads.
generation.intervention: Apply an ultrathin (approximately 10–100 nm) continuous graphene coating on the surface of the alloy using chemical vapor deposition (CVD).
generation.conditions: Tests under simultaneous applied magnetic/pressure fields and temperature cycles in the operating range of the caloric effect; mechanical compression testing at comparable strain rates to those used in previous epoxy-containing and low-melting alloy composite studies.
generation.structural_mediator: The graphene layer, due to its very high in-plane strength, toughness, and crack-arresting behavior, forms a protective, nanolaminate interface that impedes the initiation and propagation of cracks.
generation.mechanism: The continuous graphene coating redistributes local stresses and acts as a barrier to crack development without significantly impeding thermal, magnetic, or pressure-driven phase transitions responsible for the caloric effect. Its nanoscale thickness minimizes interference with the energetics of the phase transition while providing mechanical reinforcement.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the uncoated alloy, the graphene-coated samples should exhibit a marked increase in compressive strength (targeting values at or above those obtained with epoxy reinforcement, e.g., >150 MPa) and delayed crack propagation, while the magnitude of the caloric response (e.g., entropy change and induced temperature shift) remains essentially unaltered (within ±10%).
generation.baseline: The uncoated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which shows high caloric performance but low mechanical integrity (prone to cracking and relatively low compressive strength, as evidenced by the In composite and epoxy-based MM′X studies).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only if the graphene coating remains ultra‐thin (∼10–100 nm) and uniformly continuous. Excessive coating thickness or processing conditions that degrade graphene quality, or extreme operating regimes (e.g., temperatures beyond graphene’s stability window or loads that induce delamination) may negate the reinforcing effect or alter the caloric transition.
generation.uncertainty: While individual studies (e.g., PMC9227879 on graphene interfaces and the comparisons of epoxy versus low-melting In composites) support the use of nanolaminate coatings for improved mechanical integrity, it is uncertain how a graphene interlayer will interact with the specific phase transitions driving the caloric effect in MM′X alloys. This intervention extends the demonstrated crack-arresting benefits of graphene in HEA composites to a caloric material system, which remains untested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples. Coat one set with an ultrathin graphene layer via CVD and leave the other set uncoated. Subject both sets to identical mechanical compression tests and caloric effect measurements under applied magnetic/pressure fields across the relevant temperature range.
measurements: Compressive strength, strain to failure, and in-situ crack propagation (via SEM imaging)
Caloric response metrics such as isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change
Thermal and magnetic property evaluations to verify minimal interference by the coating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-coated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (e.g., a ≥20% increase in compressive strength and reduced or delayed crack formation) while retaining the caloric response within ±10% of the baseline uncoated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The compressive mechanical properties of CoCrNi/(TiC)x (x = 0, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0) composites were measured and shown in Figure 5 and Table 2. It can be seen from the figure that the introduction of the TiC ceramic phase significantly enhanced the yield strength of the composites. Compared with the yield strength of CoCrNi alloy at 108 MPa, the yield strength of samples T6, T8, and T10 increased to 883, 1102, and 1371 MPa, respectively. The increase of yield strength can be attributed to the second phase strengthening generated by TiC particles in the composites. However, the increase of TiC content led to a simultaneous decrease in the compressive strength and plasticity of the composites. Such a result is related to the microstructure change of the composites. The size of the block TiC particles that precipitated from the composites with high content of TiC addition tends to increase and connect onto pieces (Figure 3b–d), which may decrease the composite’s deformation capacity.

To reveal the underlying deformation and fracture behaviors, postmortem SEM observations were performed on the NL HEA/graphene micropillar after micro-compression testing. A representative SEM image of the NL micropillar displayed a localized shear deformation at the upper part of the HEA that yielded at 20% compressive engineering strain, as shown in Figure 5a. The side view of Figure 5b shows a few large cracks propagating along the compressive axis. It is worth mentioning that the propagation of a large crack was arrested at the graphene interface, which is evident in the enlarged image in Figure 5b. The cracking and shearing events are captured well with minor stress fluctuations in the stress–strain curve in Figure 4c. For the HEA matrix, the superior strength first was attributed to a high density of interior barriers (grain boundaries and nanotwins) for dislocation movement. Since there is relatively small grain size in CoCrFeNi HEA films, most emitted dislocations cannot accumulate within grains.
